Madeira

The Atlantic island of Madeira produces a unique fortified wine, aged oxidatively with heat, ranging from dry to sweet and famous for its vibrant acidity and extraordinary longevity.

History

The island of Madeira was settled by the Portuguese in the fifteenth century, and vines were planted soon afterwards alongside sugar cane. Its position on the Atlantic routes made Funchal a port of call for ships bound for the Americas, Africa and Asia, and the island’s wine was shipped in large quantities. It was observed that wines crossing the tropics in ships’ holds improved with the heat and motion, and this gave rise both to the practice of fortifying them with grape spirit and to techniques of ageing with heat. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Madeira was highly prized in England and in Britain’s North American colonies. In the mid-nineteenth century powdery mildew and then phylloxera destroyed much of the vineyard, which was largely replanted with Tinta Negra and other varieties.

Territory and climate

Madeira is a rugged volcanic island in the middle of the Atlantic, off the African coast. The climate is subtropical oceanic, mild and humid, with marked differences between the sunnier south side and the cooler, wetter north. Vineyards occupy small terraces, the poios, held up by stone walls on very steep slopes, and are often trained on low pergolas. Water reaches many plots through the levadas, traditional irrigation channels. The soils are volcanic, basaltic and acidic.

Winemaking

Fermentation is stopped with grape spirit at different points depending on the desired sweetness. The wine is then aged with heat in one of two ways: estufagem, in which it is heated in tanks for at least three months, used for younger wines, or the canteiro system, in which it rests for years in casks in warm lodges, reserved for the finest wines. This oxidative ageing gives Madeira great stability: an opened bottle keeps for a long time.

Grapes and styles

The traditional varieties are associated with styles of increasing sweetness: Sercial, the driest; Verdelho, medium dry; Boal (Bual), medium rich; and Malvasia (Malmsey), the sweetest. Terrantez is now very scarce. Tinta Negra is the most widely planted variety and is used in every style. Wines are also classified by age (5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 and 50 years old, among other indications), as Colheita, from a single harvest, and as Frasqueira or Garrafeira, from a single harvest and variety, with at least twenty years in wood. All share a very lively acidity that balances the sweetness. The Instituto do Vinho, do Bordado e do Artesanato da Madeira oversees the appellation, and the island also has appellations for still wines.

Country
Portugal
Climate
Subtropical oceanic, mild and humid, sunnier on the island’s south side.
Soils
Volcanic, basaltic and acidic, on terraces on steep slopes.
Styles
Oxidative fortified wines, from dry (Sercial) to sweet (Malmsey), age-dated, single-harvest (Colheita) or Frasqueira.
Grapes
Sercial, Verdelho, Malvasia
